t: Michael, thank you so much for taking the time, lovely to see you.
Thought it may be appropriate just to reflect a little bit over the last six months
and just talk about what it's been like for yourself.
I mean, if we start back in January, we were in Bob Adolph's one week,
and I know you've been asked about this quite a lot,
but then a week later you're the Manchinited head coach.
Just wondering on a human level, what was that week like for you?
Yeah, it's obviously quite a change.
What was it like? I mean, it just kind of happens so you go along with it, to be honest
with you. I don't think it's an awful lot of thinking, really. It's just natural, you
know, you kind of go along with it and get the call and discussions take place and then
you kind of just go into it. It's strange how quickly your mind flicks back into football
football mode really, from obviously going through having some time off and having Christmas
at home and having some time away with friends. My brain is a funny thing and that muscle
memory kicks in and certainly my memory kicks in and it's just what you know and flick
quite into it and obviously it was straight away into the city game, so it was quite
a fast start.
How did you find that switch you mentioned, you know, that clicks because, forget the
football for a second but just in any walk of life going from you know holiday
type environment to then into an interview process then starting a new
job I mean it's pretty pretty crazy for a week isn't it? Yeah it can be it can be I
think you just kind of try and take it step by step really and try and be
pretty clear with not get too wrapped up in everything and be try and see what
needs done, wants priorities and kind of have that priority list of whether that was going
through the process of the discussions, whether that was then getting a job to then think
well what do we need to do to prepare the players, meet the players, get to know the
players quickly, put a team together and there's kind of just prioritising of the most important
things really and that kind of cleared my head quite quickly.
And on that point, I know you quite often as a fan would go to Old Trafford with your
family to watch the game, so just wonder from your observations over the last few years
if you aren't as a fan, so then when you step into that changing room with the squad
and you're dressing them for the first time, was what you found what you expected from
just observing as a fan in the stands, or was it maybe a bit different to what you
maybe thought?
I think it's difficult, I've supported and I came through a lot of games all my underway
actually but I mean more of actually what's gone in the past on a
professional level and this level is is it's always difficult to judge from the
outside so I wouldn't I wouldn't want to go down that road but what I
certainly found is straight away was a group of players that are really
desperate to do well really good group of players and that want to stick
together with the spirit and I've spoke to it a lot of pretty much every
interview I do I talk about the spirit and the connection and I found
that straight away from the players that I was really pleased with because you
never really know somebody until you get to know somebody right so as soon
as I started to get to know the players I could see there was a real sense of
willingness to do whatever it takes to be successful which was really
pleasing. And you had a benefit of knowing some of the squad already from your
previous years here but the start you know the two outstanding wins against
Manchester City and Arsenal just wonder what do you think that did for maybe the
connection to the other backroom staff and the players who maybe they didn't
have that you know factor how much do you think that helped the players buy
into the staff and also the staff get to know the players a lot quicker as
well? I just think in every aspect it's a win and a big win and two big
wins and three big wins on the back row I think it's of course it does
wonders for everything. Staff coming in, some new staff coming into the club, getting to
know each other as well, backroom staff, course players, some I knew, some I didn't but I
didn't really. That affected me in terms of relationships from before, I think you're
coming in and judging for what it is now. But of course wins improve a lot of things
and I think it was how we achieved it. I think it was give everyone such a lift and
such a bounce and such a confidence and energy spike if you like. We kind of
tried to carry it on for as long as we could. Just alongside then and moving on
a few months, just wonder how big maybe just from the outside it felt like the
lead's defeat but then the win against Chelsea felt quite significant just
because the manner of the defeat Old Trafford but then to then win at
Chelsea for the first time and five or six years without performance. Did it
Do you feel maybe significant on the time to get back on the right road towards the Champions League football?
Not massively, really. You're going to win, hopefully you're going to win games, you're
definitely going to lose some games at some point, or the odd game here and there, we don't
want to and we certainly don't plan for it, but at some point you're going to always add setbacks
at certain times in this club, however successful we've been, so that's just part of it.
A lot of people can get carried away with it, and with the ups and the downs that's fine,
that's what some people are there for. We're certainly not. We're here to kind of understand
what we needed to do to get better. Of course the reaction is important, you know, and not
to go back to back to feet and try to keep the momentum. But it wasn't a major relief
or a major thing. It was just keep doing what we're good at and believing that we get some sort
of level of success with the results. Listen, going to Chelsea and winning, of course it
it always has been a tough place to go and winning that game was a great feeling but it wasn't so
much any bigger than it should be certainly from from inside us. I just wonder over the last
few months as the results piled up got closer to Champions League football we've spoken to
so many players over the last few months although that was our man Mateus Kinnear for example
all really supportive of you and the rest of the backroom staff so that's to continue on or just
enjoying the moment as well I mean what has that support maybe meant to you and
the staff do you think in terms of having such an impact in a short space
so I mean you mentioned kind of what a turnaround it was even to start with
yeah of course I mean we want everyone feeling in a good place and again with
a good connection and invested in each other to try and achieve something and
that's players that stuff that's all together so we want the boys to have an
element of happiness and enjoying being here. It's hard work obviously and it's
challenging and it has to be like that way but I think to be thriving in the
environment and be happy in the environment is important so you can't
always please everyone you know it's that's how it is and we're not here to
please everybody but to have to give them the opportunity and feel that they're in
a good place to perform is the most important thing. Just looking forward a
little bit I just wonder with Casamiro leaving at the end of his contract
I'm a lovely goodbyes from Old Trafford last weekend, but for Coby Manu and maybe looking
at who that ideal partner could be for him going forward in the midfield or whoever's
ever you get my point, I just wonder what qualities do you think would really compliment
Coby Manu's game as he continues to develop himself as well, whether that's in one player
or two players, in that duo?
I think Coby can do a lot of things in terms of he's got a lot of strengths and so in
in terms of whoever plays with them.
It's not all about, it's not about just bringing somebody in
to compliment Kobe, of course that's a big part
of the midfield in the balance and the whole team
of balance and who can play with and getting the best
out of each other, but I understand why you asked
that question, but I think there's a real,
to be a midfielder at Manchester, you need to have
an element of composure, an element of expression, you've got to be positive, you've got to have
an element of athleticism to deal with fast attacks and how we want to play the game,
so in the end you want to be creating excitement, you know, as well as having to defend,
so my answer is pretty much everything really, which is what you'd expect, you know, to play
the highest level and to compete for the highest honors you've got to be able to
cope with a lot of things. I just wonder your partnership with Paul
Scholes for so many years, what do you think was the key for such a
sustainable midfield partnership at this club specifically do you think? I think
there's certainly personal understanding and a wavelength of sometimes it's
coachable sometimes it's quite natural actually and seeing it over the years
with with parents whether that's centre back parents, midfield parents, striker
kind of parents sometimes things fit for a reason and certainly for playing with
scores you had a really good relationship with them understanding each
other and probably the biggest things appreciating each other's game and
trying to get the best out of each other I think all the best kind of
combinations parents units whatever that may be within a team is appreciating
and understanding each other's games certainly to try and bring out the best
in each other. I know we've asked you a lot of questions about Bruno Fernandez
over the last few months.
One thing I just wanted to ask you about
was something you mentioned at the FWA's.
So we spoke to Kieran McKenna recently
about Bruno Fernandes because you both
at the club when he first signed.
And something that stuck with me
hearing from him about Fernandes
was the training camp early in February
after he signed, I think it was in Spain.
And he just talked about his kind of recovery
and his dedication off the pitch
and kind of put him in Cristiano Ronaldo levels
of you know, world class and some of that aspect
of the game, which is maybe something we don't see as much. I mean, what were your first
impressions of Bruno at that point, you know, please?
Yeah, I mean, it's similar. I mean, it's his quality, of course, you know, I think
his natural quality on the ball and his eye for space and his eye for a pass and his
eye to be very creative. I think that's shown straight away from seeing him close up
training which obviously is why he was brought to the club in the first place and then yeah of
course the part that a lot of people get to see is what it takes at this level to be consistent
of looking after yourself, living right, doing all the right things away from the pitch and
whether that's preparation, whether that's after coming off the pitch and everything that surrounds
that live in your life, you know, there's so many things going to it and I have to say
now he's evolved into being a captain and such a leader and influential within the football
club and he carries it so well and it's not a straightforward or a natural or an easy
thing just to be able to do that but he's found a way of coping with it and now it's
natural to him and I think he represents this club in such a fantastic way.
I know we've had a bit of a speed run through the last six months, but to culminate, you
know, I know you have one more game away from home, but to culminate Old Trafford last week
and with the goodbyes to certain players, but just wonder before your speech and you're
getting serenaded by your saga.
I just wonder how much do you really feel that and does it kind of feel different, does
it impact differently as a head coach compared to when you're at Waygrounds or, you know,
that all traffered as a player in that midfield,
I imagine you maybe can't take it in all the time
when you're playing.
It was certainly a nice moment after the game,
I think, for everybody.
I felt it within the stadium,
you know, whether that was players or staff, myself,
or certainly the supporters and the friends
and the family of everybody in the stadium.
I think it was a real good feeling.
The amount of people that were there,
there was literally everyone stayed behind,
which is not always the case at different stages. The stadium was full for a long time after the
game, there was a real sense. Not that we're here to celebrate an awful lot because we were striving
for success but there was an appreciation I think of probably what the players have achieved,
where we're at, the connection with the supporters, how much they're enjoying,
watching the players perform I think is massively important of course. But then to take that
moment in the air, for sure, to be in a position I'm in and to see in the stadium and reacting
in such a way was, of course, that's very nice. And that's what pushes you on for more.
You kind of get greedy in a good way. You never take it for granted, but you get greedy
and you always want more. So to get that feeling was very nice.
Do you prefer hearing the song on the touchline or as a player?
It's just different. When you're playing and in the game, it's a different way of being
invested in the game. Physically you're writing it and you're in the heart of it, so you hear
some, you miss others. Sometimes when you're in the touch line, you're a bit more withdrawn,
so you can take a little bit more in at times, even though your eyes and your mind's on
the game. I'll probably hear it a little bit more now.
And just finally, Michael, on a personal level, what have the last six months meant to you?
I remember your first news conference, you spoke about your pride and how this is the
club for you, so the relative success, getting the team back in Champions League football
but the results, the reconnection maybe to the fans and the stands, what has all of that
meant to you over the last six months?
Oh yes, it's meant so much. It's the place that I've been in love for so long and obviously
I've been away a little bit and came back but I'm so attached to it and integrated
in the whole thing, so to be able to play a part and to see the club moving in a good
direction and, as I've said, seeing smiles on faces and the lads playing good football
and thriving and expressing themselves, you know, to be a part of that and try and lead
that and create that in a certain direction is very satisfying.
Michael, thank you so much for your time and all the best this weekend.
Cheers.
